title: Group Insurance and Government Programs
objectives: Assist clients in reviewing the main features of their group coverages.
Help clients to understand the main federal and provincial government insurance programs.
Integrate group and public (government) coverages with private insurance programs when assessing whether a client is adequately protected.

guide.heading: Group vs individual insurance
points: Clients may have protection from the private sector (group plans through employers, alumni or professional associations) or the public sector (government plans for risks, such as unemployment or retirement, that fail the criteria for insurability).

Group insurance: a master contract owned by the employer or other sponsor, usually covering several benefits (life, disability, health) on many lives. Individual insurance: owned by one person, generally one type of benefit on one life.
Employers offer group plans to attract and keep staff, to keep employees healthy and productive, and as an instrument of social policy (aiding families of disabled or deceased employees).
Premiums reflect the risk of the whole group, not the individual. Members get lower rates, no medical underwriting and often an employer subsidy.
History: fraternal groups such as the Independent Order of Foresters (1890s); Sun Life's first true group policy in Canada (1919); contributory plans by the mid-1920s.

guide.heading: Group contracts: master contract, certificate and conversion
points: Master contract: the agreement between the insurer and the sponsor (usually the employer). Generally for one year, renewable, with premium rates set for one year at a time.

Certificate of insurance: each member's evidence of coverage. It must show the insurer's name, the policy, the amounts on the member and dependants, when coverage ends and the member's rights on termination.
Member's booklet: types of benefits, who is covered and for how much, claim frequency, maximum claim limits, deductibles and co-insurance.

Conversion: usually 31 days after leaving to convert group life to permanent or one-year term with the same insurer, without medical evidence; priced on plan type, sex, smoker status and attained age.
Some plans instead continue reduced life coverage into retirement (e.g., for 5 years, reducing 20% a year). Disability and health coverage rarely have a conversion privilege.

guide.heading: Basic principles of employer/employee group plans
points: Regular employment: the member must be actively at work (not disabled) when added, a form of underwriting. Part-timers may need minimum hours (e.g., 24 a week), which also keeps premium costs in line with pay.
Type and amount of coverage are set by the master agreement, not the member, to prevent anti-selection. Flexible plans set minimum and maximum limits, and group life is usually mandatory.
The employer pays at least half of group disability costs (moral hazard: employees who pay more claim more). Non-contributory plans: employer pays all; contributory plans: employees pay up to half.
Participation: usually 75% to 100% of eligible employees, for an adequate spread of risk. In Quebec, every employee must enroll if the employer offers a group life and health plan.
Employee contributions are made by payroll deduction at source. New employees typically serve a 90-day probationary period before joining.
Other groups: associations of individuals, of employers or of franchisees; multi-employer groups (e.g., electricians, plumbers); unions; creditor groups.

guide.heading: Group life insurance
points: The cornerstone of group plans: most insurers will not issue a group contract without a mandatory group life element, while other benefits (e.g., dental) may be optional.

Amount: usually 1 or 2 times salary, often with optional extra coverage up to 5 times (e.g., $40,000 salary: $40,000 basic plus up to $160,000 optional); or a flat amount; or an amount by job category.
Basic coverage needs no proof of insurability; optional extra coverage may. Dependant coverage usually needs no evidence.
The employer usually pays for basic coverage; the employee pays (by payroll deduction) for optional coverage, including spouse and child coverage of about $5,000 to $10,000.

guide.heading: Group disability: short-term and long-term
points: Short-term (weekly indemnity): starts immediately or within 1 to 2 weeks; pays for 26 to 104 weeks; usually 100% of regular income (if the benefit is taxable); own-occupation definition.
Long-term: starts when STD ends; lasts 2 or 5 years or to age 65; pays about 70% of income if tax-free, up to 85% if taxable.
LTD uses the stricter any-occupation definition (unable to do any job suited to your education and experience), which encourages a return to gainful work.

guide.heading: Group health and cafeteria plans
points: Group health pays directly or reimburses costs not covered by provincial plans: dental, eyeglasses, prescription drugs, some hospital services. Most claims carry a deductible, co-insurance or both (dental generally both).
Traditional fixed, one-price plans make good risks subsidize poorer ones and do not fit individual needs; two-income families may also duplicate coverage.
Cafeteria plans (from the U.S., in Canada since the 1990s) give credits (e.g., $150 a month) to spend on individually priced options. Unused credits may be paid out as taxable cash.
Some coverages can be bought only with credits (life insurance usually), others with credits or payroll deduction. Benefits become more visible, and higher risks bear more of the cost.
Couples should coordinate: two 50% orthodontic coverages (up to $1,500 each) can integrate to cover $3,000 rather than duplicate.

guide.heading: Assessing group coverage: gaps, pros and cons
points: CLHIA checklist: % of income covered and dollar limits; when benefits begin; exclusions; inflation indexing; benefit period; definition of disability; partial disability; pre-existing conditions; conversion on leaving.

For individual policies also ask: are benefits paid if the client can work part-time? Can a self-employed client cover deferred tax or business expenses? Are there options for goals such as retirement saving?
Pros: lower, often employer-subsidized premiums; basic coverage without medical evidence; easy enrolment.
Cons: aggregate pricing (the healthiest members may get better individual rates); a package deal with limited choice; limited, possibly inadequate life amounts; coverage ends on leaving the group.
Do not treat group coverage, especially life insurance, as a permanent part of the plan or as the client's sole protection.

guide.heading: Tax on group premiums and benefits
points: Group life: employer-paid premiums are deductible to the employer and a taxable benefit to the employee (T4). Employee-paid premiums are generally not deductible. The death benefit is tax-free to the beneficiary.

Group disability: employer premiums are always deductible. If they are not reported as a taxable benefit, benefits are taxable; if the employee pays, or is taxed on, the premiums, benefits are tax-free.
In contributory plans, allocate the employee's contributions to the disability premium so benefits are tax-free (e.g., Paul's $40 a month covers the $35 disability premium).
Shared disability premiums, employer share not taxed: not pro rata. The employee's own premiums come back tax-free first and the rest is taxable (Ron: $4,000 tax-free and $20,000 taxable of $24,000).

Group health: employer premiums are deductible and not a taxable benefit federally, but in Quebec they are a taxable benefit for provincial income tax. Employee-paid premiums: not deductible but eligible for the medical expense tax credit. Benefits: tax-free.

guide.heading: Government programs and Old Age Security
points: Government programs cover risks beyond the individual's control that are generally uninsurable privately (premature death, old age, health, unemployment). Both levels of government run programs, sometimes similar ones.
Dominant federal programs: old age security, pensions (the CPP; Quebec has its own QPP), health care and unemployment (EI).

OAS starts at 65. Full pension: 40 years of residency (not necessarily continuous) between 18 and 65. Partial pension: at least 10 years, at 1/40 per year (25 years = 62.5%). Citizenship is not required. Indexed.
Add-ons: the Guaranteed Income Supplement (low income); the Allowance (low-income senior whose spouse/partner gets OAS and GIS); the Allowance for the Survivor.
Deferral up to 60 months: +0.6% a month, to a maximum of 36% at 70. Clawback: 15% of each taxable dollar above a threshold. OAS is taxable.

guide.heading: CPP and QPP retirement pensions
points: Mandatory participation earning employment credits (CPP everywhere except Quebec, which has the QPP); contributions are portable. Meant as basic support, topped up by private pensions and RRSPs.
Contributions: a % of income split equally by employer and employee; the self-employed pay both halves. You must be working or self-employed to contribute, so retirees stop contributing.
Pension: 25% of average monthly pensionable earnings, being enhanced to 33 1/3% (from 2019, fully by 2025; the full enhanced benefit needs about 40 years of enhanced contributions). Indexed.
Start between 60 and 70 (normal 65). CPP early: −0.6% a month (−36% at 60). QPP early: −0.5% to −0.6% a month by pension size (−30% to −36% at 60). Late: +0.7% a month (+42% at 70).

Pension sharing: both spouses 60+; both pensions shared if both receive one; must apply (not via CRA pension income splitting); only credits earned together, up to 50%; each is taxed on his or her share. Credits can also be split on divorce or separation.

guide.heading: CPP/QPP disability and death benefits
points: Benefits also go to disabled contributors and to surviving spouses and children. Lump-sum death benefit: up to $2,500. All CPP/QPP benefits, including the death benefit, are taxable.

Disability pension: for a severe and prolonged physical or mental condition preventing regular work at any job. Starts after 4 months; paid to 65, when the retirement pension begins. Children: under 18, or 18 to 25 in full-time school.

CPP eligibility: contributions in 4 of the last 6 calendar years, or 25 years including 3 of the last 6. QPP eligibility: 2 of the last 3 years, 5 of the last 10, or half the contributory period (at least 2 years).
Many people disabled for other purposes will not meet the strict definition, so do not count on this benefit to meet disability needs.

guide.heading: Health care, EI and other federal programs
points: Health care: the federal government started the national program, but provinces now administer it, funding is shifting to the provincial tax base, and it is becoming increasingly unique to each province.

EI is the core federal program. Sickness benefits: from the 15th day of illness, disability or quarantine, for 15 weeks; enough insurable weeks or hours are needed; some self-employed can register for special benefits. All EI benefits are taxable.

EI is a second payer: CPP/QPP, Workers' Compensation or group plan income reduces it dollar for dollar, but individual disability policy benefits do not. Starting group benefits after EI ends (17 weeks) maximizes total income.
Not all federal insurance is social: the Export Development Corporation, a federal Crown corporation, insures exporters against off-shore buyers who fail to pay.

guide.heading: Provincial programs
points: Provinces focus on health care (with growing administrative and financial responsibility), workers' compensation, social services (welfare, help with substance abuse, job training and re-entry) and agriculture.

Workers' Compensation (WCB or WSIB) covers work-related accidents and illness: typically 90% of average weekly earnings after income tax, CPP/QPP and EI, paid tax-free from the date of disability until return to work; may include retraining.
Employers pay all WC premiums (salary-based, varying by industry). They are deductible to the employer and not a taxable benefit to employees.
Agriculture: hail and crop insurance. AgriInsurance is a federal-provincial-producer cost-shared program delivered by each province that stabilizes income after natural-hazard losses.
Many clients and planners leave government retirement benefits out of long-term plans because of uncertainty about long-term funding.

tips: EXAM TIP: Employer-paid group life premiums are a taxable benefit to the employee, but the death benefit is tax-free to the beneficiary.
EXAM TIP: Group disability benefits are tax-free only if the employee paid, or was taxed on, the premiums; otherwise they are taxable.
EXAM TIP: Shared disability premiums aren't taxed pro rata: the employee's own premiums come back tax-free first, the rest is taxable.
EXAM TIP: Employer-paid health premiums aren't a taxable benefit federally, but in Quebec they are taxable for provincial income tax.
EXAM TIP: Short-term disability uses own occupation; long-term disability uses the stricter any occupation definition.
EXAM TIP: OAS needs 40 years' residency between 18 and 65 for a full pension; each year earns 1/40, with at least 10 years for a partial one.
EXAM TIP: CPP early start costs 0.6% a month (36% at 60); a late start adds 0.7% a month (42% at 70). QPP early: 0.5% to 0.6% a month.
DID YOU KNOW? In Quebec, every employee of an employer offering a group life and health plan must join it; elsewhere 75% to 100% is typical.
EXAM TIP: EI sickness benefits start on day 15, last 15 weeks and are second payer, except to individual disability policies.
DID YOU KNOW? Workers' compensation typically pays 90% of net earnings tax-free, and the employer pays the entire premium.

flashcards.front: Three reasons employers set up group plans
flashcards.back: 1) An incentive for employees to join or stay. 2) A way to keep employees healthy and productive. 3) An instrument of social policy, aiding the families of disabled or deceased employees.

flashcards.front: Group certificate of insurance: required contents
flashcards.back: The insurer's name; identification of the policy; the amount of insurance on the member and dependants; when the insurance terminates; and the insured's rights on termination.

Usually 31 days after leaving the group to convert to permanent or one-year term insurance with the same insurer, without medical evidence. The premium is based on plan type, sex, smoker status and attained age.

flashcards.front: Six basic principles of employer/employee group plans
flashcards.back: Actively at work when added; type and amount set by the master agreement; employer pays at least half of disability cost; minimum participation; contributions by payroll deduction; a probationary period before joining.
Usually 75% to 100% of eligible employees must join, for an adequate spread of risk. In Quebec, every employee of an employer offering a group life and health plan must enroll.

flashcards.front: Typical probationary period for new employees
flashcards.back: 90 days. It discourages people from taking a job just to get benefits such as dental, and reduces claims and administration costs.

flashcards.front: Types of groups besides employer/employee plans
flashcards.back: Associations of individuals (e.g., lawyers), associations of employers, associations of franchisees, multi-employer groups (e.g., electricians, plumbers), unions and creditor groups.

flashcards.front: Three ways to set group life amounts
flashcards.back: A multiple of salary (usually 1 or 2 times, with optional extra often up to 5 times in total); a flat amount for every member; or an amount by job category.
Starts immediately or within 1 to 2 weeks; pays for 26 to 104 weeks; usually 100% of regular pre-disability income (if taxable); uses the own-occupation definition.
Starts when STD ends and lasts 2 or 5 years or to age 65. Pays about 70% of income if tax-free or up to 85% if taxable. Uses the stricter any-occupation definition.

Own occupation: disabled if unable to do any duties of your regular occupation (or able to do them only part of the time). Any occupation: disabled only if unable to do any job suited to your education and experience.
Members get credits (e.g., $150 a month) to spend on individually priced coverage options; unused credits may be paid out as taxable cash. Life insurance can usually be bought only with credits.

flashcards.front: Tax on group life premiums and death benefits
flashcards.back: Employer-paid premiums: deductible to the employer and a taxable benefit to the employee (T4). Employee-paid premiums: generally not deductible. Death benefit: tax-free to the beneficiary.

Employer-paid premiums not reported as a taxable benefit: benefits are taxable. Premiums paid by the employee, or taxed to him or her: benefits are tax-free. The employer deducts its premiums either way.

flashcards.front: Shared disability premiums: how benefits are taxed
flashcards.back: Not pro rata. If the employer's share is not taxed to the employee, the employee's own premiums come back first as tax-free benefits and the rest of the benefits are taxable.

flashcards.front: Tax on group health premiums and benefits
flashcards.back: Employer-paid: deductible, and not a taxable benefit federally, but taxable for Quebec income tax. Employee-paid: not deductible, but eligible for the medical expense tax credit. Benefits: tax-free.

flashcards.front: Advantages and drawbacks of group insurance
flashcards.back: Pros: lower, often subsidized premiums; basic coverage without medical evidence; easy enrolment. Cons: aggregate pricing; a package deal with little choice; limited life amounts; ends when you leave the group.
Full pension: 40 years of residency (not necessarily continuous) between ages 18 and 65. Partial pension: at least 10 years, at 1/40 of the full pension per year. Citizenship is not required.
Deferral up to 60 months: +0.6% a month, to a maximum of 36% at 70. Clawback: 15% of each taxable dollar above a set income threshold. OAS is taxable.

flashcards.front: GIS, Allowance and Allowance for the Survivor
flashcards.back: GIS: for low-income OAS pensioners. Allowance: low-income seniors whose spouse or partner receives or is eligible for OAS and GIS. Allowance for the Survivor: low-income seniors whose spouse or partner has died and who have not repartnered.
Mandatory (CPP everywhere except Quebec, which has the QPP), with portable credits. Contributions are a percentage of income split equally by employer and employee; the self-employed pay both halves.
Normal age 65; earliest 60, latest 70. CPP early: −0.6% a month (−36% at 60). QPP early: −0.5% to −0.6% a month by pension size (−30% to −36% at 60). Late: +0.7% a month (+42% at 70).
25% of average monthly pensionable earnings, being enhanced to 33 1/3% (from 2019, fully in place by 2025; the full enhanced benefit needs about 40 years of enhanced contributions). Indexed.

Both spouses 60 or older; if both receive pensions, both must be shared; must apply (not through CRA pension income splitting); only credits earned while together, up to 50%; each is taxed on his or her share.
A one-time lump sum of up to $2,500 on the death of a qualified contributor. Taxable, like all CPP/QPP benefits.
CPP: contributions in 4 of the last 6 calendar years, or 25 years including 3 of the last 6. QPP: 2 of the last 3 years, or 5 of the last 10, or half the contributory period (at least 2 years).

For a severe and prolonged condition preventing regular work at any job. Taxable; starts after 4 months; paid to 65, when the retirement pension begins. Children: under 18, or 18 to 25 in full-time school.
From the 15th day of disability, for 15 weeks; taxable. Second payer: CPP/QPP, Workers' Compensation or group plan income reduces EI dollar for dollar, but individual disability policies do not.
Typically 90% of average weekly earnings after income tax, CPP/QPP and EI; tax-free from the date of disability until return to work. Employers pay all premiums (deductible; not a taxable benefit).

A federal-provincial-producer cost-shared program developed and delivered by each province. It stabilizes farm income by limiting the economic effects of production and quality losses caused by natural hazards.

Federal: old age security, pensions (the CPP; Quebec has its own QPP), health care (initial sponsor) and unemployment (EI). Provincial: health care administration, workers' compensation, social services and agriculture.

flashcards.front: Can a retiree keep contributing to the CPP/QPP?
flashcards.back: No. You must be working or self-employed to contribute, so once retired you no longer qualify as a contributor.

questions.q: How are premiums for an employer group plan determined, compared with individual insurance?
options: By each member's medical exam results, averaged across the group
By each member's age, sex and smoking status, priced one by one
By the risk of the group as a whole, not each member's own risk
By the employer's credit rating and the size of its total payroll
questions.explain: Group premiums are governed by the risk of the group as a whole, and a large number of members softens the insurer's risk. That is why basic group coverage can be offered at lower rates without medical underwriting.

questions.q: An employer says its group plan exists partly to help the families of employees who become disabled or die. Which of the course's three reasons for group plans does this reflect?
options: Acting as an instrument of social policy
Attracting new employees and retaining staff
Keeping employees healthy and productive
Supplementing employees' retirement income
questions.explain: The three reasons are: an incentive to join or stay with the employer, a way to keep employees healthy and productive, and an instrument of social policy to aid families of disabled or deceased employees. Retirement income belongs to pension plans.

questions.q: Because the group master contract is between the insurer and the employer, what serves as each plan member's evidence of insurance?
options: A copy of the master contract countersigned by the employer
The plan member's booklet, issued by the employer's HR team
The member's T4 slip showing the taxable premium for the year
A certificate of insurance issued to the member by the insurer
questions.explain: The insurer issues each member a certificate showing the insurer, the policy, the coverage on the member and dependants, when coverage ends and the member's rights on termination. The booklet only summarizes the benefits.

questions.q: Kevin leaves his employer. Under a typical group life conversion privilege, what can he do?
options: Convert within 90 days, provided he passes a full medical examination
Convert within 31 days to an individual policy with no medical evidence
Keep his group coverage at the same group rate for the rest of his life
Convert only to permanent coverage, priced at his age when he was hired
questions.explain: Group life usually lets a departing member convert within 31 days to permanent or one-year term insurance with the same insurer, without evidence of insurability. The premium is based on the plan, sex, smoker status and attained age at conversion.

questions.q: Why must an employee be actively at work, not off on disability, on the day he or she is added to the group policy?
options: It ensures premiums can be collected through payroll deduction from day one
It acts as a form of underwriting, since working shows a measure of good health
It prevents anti-selection by letting each member pick his or her own coverage amounts
It is required so that the employer can deduct its share of the premiums
questions.explain: Basic group coverage is issued without medical underwriting, so requiring regular attendance at work on enrollment keeps the insurer from taking on too many poor risks. A disabled employee must wait until returning to regular work.

questions.q: A plan covers part-time staff only if they work at least 24 hours a week. Besides showing the worker is healthy enough to work regularly, what does this rule achieve?
options: It ensures part-timers qualify for EI sickness benefits first
It lets the insurer skip the actively-at-work requirement
It allows part-timers to choose their own amounts of coverage
It keeps the employer's premium cost reasonable relative to pay
questions.explain: A minimum-hours rule keeps premium costs in line with compensation: giving identical health benefits to a 10-hour and a 40-hour employee would cost the employer four times as much per hour worked for the part-timer.

questions.q: Why is each member's type and amount of group coverage set by the master agreement rather than chosen freely by the member?
options: To avoid anti-selection, where the least healthy pick coverages they'll claim on
To ensure every member pays exactly the same premium as the employer does
To let the employer deduct the full premium cost of the plan for income tax purposes
To make sure all coverages can be converted without evidence of insurability
questions.explain: With free choice, the least healthy would pick the coverages they expect to claim (e.g., older employees choosing life insurance), making claims unpredictable and costly. Flexible plans still set minimum and maximum limits.

questions.q: Why do group plans generally require the employer to pay at least half of the cost of group disability coverage?
options: Only disability premiums paid by an employer are deductible for income tax purposes
Disability benefits must be taxable for the plan to count as a group plan
Employees who pay most of the cost tend to claim more, a form of moral hazard
Insurers cannot collect more than half of any premium through payroll
questions.explain: Studies show that when employees pay more than half the disability premium, claims rise disproportionately as they try to get their money's worth. Disability cover is also expensive, so the employer's share keeps employee contributions low.

questions.q: In Quebec, employees may opt out of their employer's group life and health plan, as long as at least 75% of eligible employees enroll.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Insurers typically require 75% to 100% participation, but Quebec legislation requires every employee of an employer that offers a group life and health plan to enroll as a member.

questions.q: What is the typical probationary (waiting) period before a new employee can join an existing group plan?
options: 31 days
15 days
17 weeks
90 days
questions.explain: A probationary period, typically 90 days, discourages people from taking a job just to access benefits such as dental and reduces claims and administration costs. The 31 days is the usual group life conversion window.

questions.q: How is a plan member's basic group life coverage most commonly calculated?
options: As career-average earnings times years of service
As a fixed $5,000 to $10,000 for every member
As one or two times the member's current salary
As 70% to 85% of the member's pre-disability pay
questions.explain: Basic group life is usually one or two times salary, often with optional extra coverage up to five times salary. Some plans use a flat amount or amounts by job category; $5,000 to $10,000 is typical of optional dependant coverage.

questions.q: Rina earns $55,000. Her plan gives basic life coverage of two times salary and lets members buy optional coverage up to a total of five times salary. What is the most optional coverage she can add?
questions.explain: Five times salary is $275,000 in total. Basic coverage is 2 × $55,000 = $110,000, so the optional coverage is $275,000 − $110,000 = $165,000, the same method as the course's one-times-basic, four-times-optional example.

questions.q: Which statement about medical evidence under a group life plan is correct?
options: All group life coverage requires a medical exam at the time of enrolment
Basic coverage needs no medical proof, but extra optional coverage may
Dependant coverage needs medical proof, but the member's basic does not
Optional coverage never needs proof, but basic coverage always requires it
questions.explain: Basic group life is provided without proof of insurability, but members may need medical evidence to take extra optional coverage, depending on the plan. Coverage on dependants is usually provided without evidence.

questions.q: Marco, a surgeon, injures his hand. He cannot operate but could teach at a medical school. Under the definitions most group plans use, how is his claim likely to be treated?
options: STD may stop under an any-occupation test; LTD pays under an own-occupation test
Both STD and LTD pay, since both use the own-occupation definition of disability
STD pays under an own-occupation test; LTD may stop under an any-occupation test
Neither pays, since both use the stricter any-occupation definition of disability
questions.explain: Short-term disability usually uses own occupation (unable to do the duties of your regular job), so Marco qualifies. Long-term disability usually uses the stricter any-occupation test, and he can do other work suited to his education and experience.

questions.q: Why do group LTD benefits typically replace about 70% of income in some plans but up to 85% in others?
options: About 70% applies if benefits are tax-free; up to 85% if they are taxable
About 70% applies to own-occupation claims; 85% to any-occupation claims
About 70% applies to part-time staff; up to 85% to full-time employees
About 70% applies before age 55; up to 85% from age 55 until age 65
questions.explain: LTD usually pays 70% to 85% of pre-disability income: about 70% when benefits are received tax-free and up to 85% when they are taxable. Short-term disability often pays 100% of regular income when the benefit is taxable.

questions.q: Which statement about group health benefit claims, such as dental or prescription drugs, is correct?
options: They are paid in full with no cost-sharing, as provincial plans require
Only hospital services already covered by the provincial plan are eligible
One flat deductible applies to every type of benefit in the same way
Most are subject to a deductible, co-insurance or both, varying by benefit
questions.explain: Most health claims carry a deductible, a co-insurance factor or both, and these vary with the type of benefit claimed; dental coverage generally has both. Group health pays for costs not covered by provincial medical plans.

questions.q: What is the key feature of a cafeteria approach to group benefits?
options: Every member gets the same fixed schedule of benefits at a single price
Members get credits to spend on individually priced coverage options
Premiums for every coverage are blended across all members of the group
Members may pick any coverage with no minimum or maximum benefit limits
questions.explain: Cafeteria plans give members credits (e.g., $150 a month) to allocate among individually priced options, so higher risks such as smokers pay more. The traditional fixed, blended approach makes good risks subsidize poorer ones.

questions.q: Leah and Sam each have cafeteria plans whose dental option pays 50% of restorative orthodontics, up to $1,500 a year. Their child needs $3,000 of such work this year. What should they do?
options: Only one elects it, since the second plan's coverage would be wasted
Both elect the option, so the two plans together cover the full $3,000
Only one elects it, and that plan will then pay the whole $3,000 bill
Neither elects it, since orthodontics can only be bought by payroll deduction
questions.explain: Electing the same coverage is not always wasteful duplication. Here the two plans integrate: each pays half, up to $1,500, so together they cover the full $3,000.

questions.q: In a cafeteria plan, members can usually pay for life insurance either with their benefit credits or by payroll deduction.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Some coverages can be bought with credits or by payroll deduction, but life insurance can usually only be paid for with credits; restricting certain coverages to credits limits their use.

questions.q: A planner is checking whether a client's group disability coverage is adequate. Which question comes from the CLHIA checklist the course cites?
options: Is the group insurer federally chartered?
Does the employer pay 75% of the premium?
Is the plan sold through a general agency?
Are the benefits indexed to inflation?
questions.explain: The checklist asks about the percentage of income covered, when benefits begin, exclusions, inflation indexing, how long benefits last, the definition of disability, partial disability, pre-existing condition clauses and conversion on leaving.

questions.q: An employer pays the premiums for an employee's group life coverage. How are those premiums treated for tax?
options: Deductible to the employer and a taxable benefit to the employee
Deductible to the employer and not a taxable benefit to the employee
Not deductible to the employer but a taxable benefit to the employee
Not deductible to the employer and not a taxable benefit to the employee
questions.explain: Employer-paid group life premiums are deductible to the employer and are a taxable benefit to the employee, reported on the T4. Group life premiums the employee pays personally are generally not deductible.

questions.q: Nadia's employer paid $300 of group life premiums last year for her $150,000 of coverage. She died in December, and her husband, the beneficiary, received $150,000. What are the tax results?
options: The $150,000 is taxable to her estate; the $300 is not taxable to anyone
Both amounts are tax-free because Nadia died before the year ended
The $300 is taxable to Nadia on her final return; the $150,000 is tax-free
The $300 is taxable to her husband; the $150,000 is taxable to her estate
questions.explain: The employer deducts the $300, which is a taxable benefit reported on Nadia's terminal return. The group life death benefit is tax-free to the beneficiary and is not a taxable benefit to Nadia or her estate.

questions.q: An employer pays the full group disability premium and does not report it as a taxable benefit to employees. How are disability benefits taxed when paid?
options: They are received tax-free by the employee
Only the portion above 70% of pay is taxable
They are taxable only after the first 17 weeks
They are taxable income to the employee
questions.explain: When the employer pays the disability premium and it is not reported as a taxable benefit, benefits are taxable. If the employee pays the premium, or the employer's premium is reported as a taxable benefit, benefits are tax-free.

questions.q: Jon's group plan costs $120 a month, $50 of which is for disability coverage. Jon contributes $60 a month. How can the plan be set up so that any disability benefits he receives are tax-free?
options: Split every premium 50/50 so that half of each benefit is tax-free
Have the employer pay the disability premium and deduct it as an expense
Allocate $50 of Jon's contribution to pay the entire disability premium
Use Jon's $60 for the health and life premiums, which makes benefits tax-free
questions.explain: In a contributory plan, the employee's contributions can be allocated to pay all of the disability premium, so disability benefits are received tax-free. Splitting premiums does not make benefits tax-free pro rata.

questions.q: Ana and her employer have each paid $3,000 of group disability premiums since the plan began; the employer's share was never reported as a taxable benefit. Ana now receives $18,000 of disability benefits. How much is taxable?
questions.explain: Shared premiums are not taxed pro rata. Ana's own $3,000 of premiums comes back first as tax-free benefits, and the remaining $15,000 is taxable income.

questions.q: For federal income tax, how are employer-paid group health premiums (e.g., dental) and the benefits paid under the plan treated?
options: Deductible to the employer and a taxable benefit; benefits are tax-free
Deductible to the employer, not a taxable benefit; benefits are tax-free
Deductible to the employer, not a taxable benefit; benefits are taxable
Not deductible to the employer, not a taxable benefit; benefits taxable
questions.explain: Federally, employer-paid health premiums are deductible for the employer and not a taxable benefit for the employee, and health benefits are received tax-free whoever pays. Quebec's provincial income tax is the exception.

questions.q: Sylvie works in Montreal, and her employer pays her group dental premiums. How are those premiums treated for income tax?
options: Taxable federally, but not a taxable benefit for Quebec income tax
A taxable benefit for both federal and Quebec income tax purposes
Not taxable federally, but a taxable benefit for Quebec income tax
Not a taxable benefit for either federal or Quebec income tax
questions.explain: For Quebec provincial income tax, premiums an employer pays for health care coverage such as dental are a taxable benefit to the employee in the year paid. Federally, they are not a taxable benefit. The benefits themselves stay tax-free.

questions.q: Group health premiums that an employee pays personally are not tax-deductible, but they qualify for the medical expense tax credit.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Employee-paid health premiums are not deductible but do qualify for the medical expense tax credit. Either way, benefits paid under the plan are received tax-free.

questions.q: Because group coverage ends when a member leaves the group, it is risky for a client to treat group life insurance as a permanent, sole source of protection.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Group coverage terminates when the member resigns, retires or is terminated, and group life amounts are limited and may be inadequate, so it should not be relied on as the client's only protection.

questions.q: Alfred immigrated to Canada at age 29 and has lived here since. He plans to retire at 60. When can his OAS pension start, and roughly what share of the full pension will he get?
options: At 65, about 90% of the full pension (36 of 40 years)
At 60, about 80% of the full pension (32 of 40 years)
At 65, the full pension, since he has over 10 years
At 65, nothing, since he lacks 40 years of residency
questions.explain: OAS starts at 65 whenever he retires. It depends on residency between 18 and 65, not working years: by 65 Alfred will have 36 years, earning 36/40 = 90%. At least 10 years of residency qualifies for a partial pension.

questions.q: Felix delays the start of his OAS pension from age 65 to age 70. Using the course's figures, how much larger will his monthly pension be?
options: 42% larger
30% larger
60% larger
36% larger
questions.explain: OAS can be deferred up to 60 months, with the pension increased by 0.6% per month of delay, to a maximum of 36% at age 70. The 42% figure is the CPP/QPP increase for deferring to 70.

questions.q: How does the OAS clawback reduce benefits for higher-income recipients?
options: By 50% of each dollar of taxable income above a set threshold
By 15% of each dollar of taxable income above a set threshold
By cancelling OAS entirely once income passes a set threshold
By 15% of the pension, because OAS is otherwise received tax-free
questions.explain: The clawback recovers 15% of each taxable dollar earned above a prescribed income threshold and can reduce or eliminate OAS for high earners. OAS itself is taxable to the recipient.

questions.q: How do CPP/QPP contributions for a self-employed person compare with those of an employee earning the same income?
options: The self-employed person pays half of what the employee contributes
The self-employed person pays both halves, twice the employee's share
Both pay the same; the government covers the missing employer share
The self-employed person is exempt and does not contribute at all
questions.explain: Contributions are a percentage of income, shared equally by employer and employee. A self-employed person must pay the entire contribution, so pays twice what an employee with the same income pays.

questions.q: Owen's CPP pension at 65 would be $1,000 a month. He starts it the month he turns exactly 63. Using the course's CPP reduction rule, what will he receive?
options: $880 a month
$928 a month
$832 a month
$856 a month
questions.explain: CPP is reduced 0.6% for each month before 65. Owen is 24 months early: 24 × 0.6% = 14.4%, so $1,000 × 85.6% = $856. A 0.5% monthly rate (the low end of the QPP range) would give $880.

questions.q: How does the early-start reduction for the QPP retirement pension differ from the CPP's, according to the course?
options: QPP: 0.5% to 0.6% a month depending on pension size; CPP: 0.6% a month
QPP: 0.7% a month for every pensioner; CPP: 0.6% a month for everyone
QPP: no early pension at all; CPP: 0.6% a month from as early as age 60
QPP: 0.6% a month for everyone; CPP: 0.5% to 0.6% depending on size
questions.explain: In Quebec, the QPP reduction is 0.5% a month for a very small pension and 0.6% for the maximum pension, so starting at 60 cuts it by 30% to 36%. The CPP reduction is 0.6% a month, or 36% at 60.

questions.q: A CPP or QPP retirement pension started at age 70 is 42% larger than one started at 65, because it rises 0.7% for each month of delay.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Deferral adds 0.7% a month (8.4% a year), so waiting the full 60 months to age 70 adds 42%. The pension can start as early as 60 or as late as 70.

questions.q: Lise, 66, receives a CPP pension of $8,000 a year and her husband Marc, 64, receives $2,000. All their credits were earned while married. If they apply to share their pensions, what will each receive?
options: Lise $4,000 and Marc $6,000
Lise $6,000 and Marc $4,000
$5,000 a year each
No change; both must be 65 or older
questions.explain: Sharing requires both spouses to be at least 60, and since both receive pensions, both must be split. Lise's $8,000 gives $4,000 each and Marc's $2,000 gives $1,000 each, so each receives, and is taxed on, $5,000.

questions.q: Spouses can share their CPP/QPP retirement pensions simply by electing the Canada Revenue Agency's pension income splitting on their tax returns.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Couples must apply to share their retirement pensions; it cannot be done through the CRA's pension income splitting program. Only pensions earned while married or living together can be shared, to a maximum of 50%.

questions.q: Which contribution rule applies to the QPP disability benefit, as opposed to the CPP disability pension?
options: Contributions in at least 4 of the last 6 calendar years
Contributions for 25 years, including 3 of the last 6
Contributions in at least 10 of the last 15 years
Contributions in at least 2 of the last 3 years
questions.explain: In Quebec, QPP eligibility is 2 of the last 3 years, or 5 of the last 10, or at least half the contributory period (minimum 2 years). The CPP requires 4 of the last 6 calendar years, or 25 years of contributions including 3 of the last 6.

questions.q: Which statement about CPP/QPP disability benefits is correct?
options: They begin on the 15th day of disability and are tax-free
They begin immediately and continue for life, tax-free
They begin after four months of disability and are taxable
They begin after four months and stop at age 60
questions.explain: CPP/QPP disability benefits start after four months, are taxable and continue to 65, when the retirement pension begins. They require a severe and prolonged condition preventing regular work at any job, so many disabled people won't qualify.

questions.q: Which statement about Employment Insurance sickness benefits is correct?
options: They start on the 15th day of disability, last 15 weeks and are taxable
They start after four months of disability, and they are received tax-free
They start on the first day, last up to 17 weeks and are tax-free
They start on the 15th day and continue to age 65 as taxable income
questions.explain: EI sickness benefits begin from the 15th day of disability and are payable for 15 weeks, and all EI benefits are taxable. Medical proof may be required, and claimants need enough weeks or hours of insurable employment.

questions.q: Pat is off work sick and claiming EI sickness benefits. Which of these other income sources would NOT reduce his EI benefit?
options: Benefits from his employer's group disability plan
Benefits from an individual disability policy he owns
A CPP/QPP disability benefit paid for the same period
Workers' Compensation benefits for the same period
questions.explain: EI is a second payer: income from CPP/QPP, Workers' Compensation or a group plan reduces EI dollar for dollar. The exception is coverage under an individual disability policy, which does not reduce EI.

questions.q: An employer is redesigning its group short-term disability plan. Which design does the course say produces higher total disability income for employees?
options: Group benefits that start on day one and run alongside EI benefits
Group benefits that replace EI so employees stop paying EI premiums
Group benefits that start only after EI sickness benefits run out
Group benefits paid only if a CPP/QPP disability claim is refused
questions.explain: Because EI is a second payer, group benefits paid at the same time simply reduce EI. Plans whose benefits begin only after EI runs out (17 weeks after disability starts) give the employee more total income.

questions.q: Using the course's typical Workers' Compensation formula, what weekly benefit would a worker earning $1,000 a week receive if deductions are $180 income tax, $50 CPP/QPP and $16 EI?
questions.explain: The typical benefit is 90% of average weekly earnings after income tax, CPP/QPP and EI: ($1,000 − $180 − $50 − $16) × 0.9 = $754 × 0.9 = $678.60. It is paid tax-free.

questions.q: Which statement about Workers' Compensation is correct?
options: Employees and employers share the premiums, and benefits are taxable
The province pays premiums from general revenue; benefits are taxable
Employees pay premiums by payroll deduction; benefits are tax-free
Employers pay all the premiums, and benefits are received tax-free
questions.explain: Employers pay salary-based premiums, which can vary by industry; they are deductible to the employer and not a taxable benefit to employees. Benefits are tax-free from the date of disability until the worker returns to work.

questions.q: Sean, 24, is reluctant to join his group plan because he must pay tax on the employer-paid premiums. Which response from his planner reflects the course?
options: He can deduct the taxable premiums on his own tax return, so there is no net cost to him
Tax costs only part of the premium, and taxed disability premiums mean tax-free benefits
Group premiums are never a taxable benefit to employees, so he has simply been misinformed
He should decline, since individual coverage is always cheaper for healthy young people
questions.explain: A taxable benefit costs him only the tax on the premium (about 30% to 40% of it), not the whole premium. And if employer-paid disability premiums are taxed to him, any disability benefits are tax-free. Group coverage also needs no underwriting.
